name: baysor
desc: Bayesian segmentation of imaging-based spatial transcriptomics data
why: Bayesian cell segmentation of spatial transcriptomics data is real science you can run, though it needs suitable data to enjoy.

brief.what_it_is: Baysor is a command-line tool for cell segmentation of imaging-based spatial transcriptomics data. It takes a molecule table with x, y and gene columns (z optional for 3D) and assigns each detected molecule to a cell, using molecule positions and gene composition. It can run with or without a prior segmentation. The output goes to a directory, default 'segmentation'. The current release is the native C++ version, cpp-0.9.0, and the executable is baysor.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as finding cells from molecule positions and gene composition, with or without a prior segmentation, in imaging-based spatial transcriptomics, where cell boundaries are hard to define from the molecule data alone.
brief.how_it_works: The README describes a Bayesian segmentation model over molecule positions and gene identities. The user supplies an approximate cell radius (-s) and a minimum molecule count per cell (-m), or a prior segmentation as a second input with --prior-segmentation-confidence (default 0.2). The README does not go into more detail on the model.

commands_seen.context: Downloads the Linux x86-64 release archive from the cpp-0.9.0 GitHub release.
Runs segmentation on molecules.csv with -m 30 (minimum molecules per cell) and -s 8 (approximate cell radius). The README calls 30 and 8 examples, not defaults.
Runs the same segmentation through the pinned 0.9.0 Docker image, from the directory containing molecules.csv.
Source build on Linux or macOS using a private conda-forge environment, with no root needed. Installs the binary to install/bin.
Checks the version of a source-built binary.
Clones the cpp-0.9.0 tag for a source build.

brief.install_notes: Release binaries exist for Linux x86-64 (glibc 2.28 or newer), macOS 12+ on Apple Silicon (arm64), and 64-bit Windows 10+ (zip; keep the DLLs beside baysor.exe). No Intel-Mac binary is listed. Docker image is Linux x86-64 only, runs as UID/GID 1000 unless you pass --user. Source builds need a C++17 compiler, CMake 3.20+, Eigen, spdlog, CGAL, Arrow/Parquet, HDF5, nlohmann_json, libtiff and zlib; configure.sh can fetch these via conda, vcpkg, or use system packages. The Ubuntu 24.04 route needs the Apache Arrow apt repository added first. No account or licence key was mentioned. The -c flag takes a TOML config file, and --threads defaults to physical cores.
brief.standout: It takes a prior segmentation as an optional second input and lets you weight it with a confidence setting, so it can refine an existing segmentation or run from molecules alone. The project also ships a 'segfree' mode and a 'preview' command, though the README doesn't explain either.
brief.status: Appears active: a versioned C++ release (cpp-0.9.0), pinned Docker tags, and versioned docs with a latest track. I did not see a release date or last-commit date, so recency is unknown. The old Julia v0.7.1 line is archived and the README warns not to install it unpinned.
brief.caveats: Parameters must be chosen for the protocol; the README stresses that 30 and 8 are examples. Platform coverage is limited: no Intel Mac binary is listed. Source builds have a heavy dependency list. The Docker image is x86-64 Linux only. Legacy Julia users are pointed to a migration guide. The brew scout note says it needs suitable data. I did not check the licence file.
quotes: Baysor finds cells from molecule positions and gene composition, with or without a prior segmentation.
The table needs `x`, `y` and `gene` columns (optional `z` for 3D).
`30` molecules and radius `8` are examples, not universal settings.
Do not use an unpinned Julia package install: the default branch is now C++.
